title: Why Twenty Amos? — Three Reasons
subtitle: The opening Mishnah, and three sages' three different sources for the same height limit.
sources: Mishnah + Gemara text: Sefaria (William Davidson Edition). Structure cross-checked against the Dafyomi Advancement Forum (dafyomi.co.il) overview, points-to-ponder, and Talmud Navigator for Sukkah 2. Tosfos: dafyomi.co.il's "Point by Point Summary of Tosfos" (Yaakov Montrose, Kollel Iyun Hadaf).

mishnah.he: סוּכָּה שֶׁהִיא גְּבוֹהָה לְמַעְלָה מֵעֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה — פְּסוּלָה. וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה מַכְשִׁיר. וְשֶׁאֵינָהּ גְּבוֹהָה עֲשָׂרָה טְפָחִים, וְשֶׁאֵין לָהּ שָׁלֹשׁ דְּפָנוֹת, וְשֶׁחֲמָתָהּ מְרוּבָּה מְצִלָּתָהּ — פְּסוּלָה.
mishnah.gloss: A sukkah that is more than twenty amos high is unfit — Rabbi Yehuda deems it fit. Likewise a sukkah that is not even ten tefachim high, or that does not have three walls, or whose sunlight passing through its roofing is greater than its shade — unfit.

flow.label: Gemara compares: an over-height mavoy (alleyway) is fixed; an over-height sukkah is just "unfit"
Answer: sukkah is Torah law (d'Oraisa), taught as simply unfit; mavoy is only rabbinic, taught as fixable
Gemara asks: from where is the 20-amos law itself derived?

flowCaption: Same halachic line, three different derivations — Abaye tests two of them immediately.

opinions.claim: A sukkah over 20 amos high is unfit — stated without qualification in the Mishnah.
Deems it fit. (His fuller position — fit up to 40–50 amos, argued from Queen Helene's sukkah — is developed on 2b.)

Derives the line from "so that your future generations will know that I caused the children of Israel to reside in sukkot" (Vayikra 23:43). Up to 20 amos a person's eye catches the roofing without effort; above it, the eye doesn't, and the awareness the verse requires is lost.

Derives the line from "and there shall be a sukkah for shade in the daytime from the heat" (Yeshayahu 4:6). Up to 20 amos a person sits in the shade of the sukkah's own roofing; above it, any shade comes from the walls instead.

Derives the line from "in sukkot shall you reside seven days" (Vayikra 23:42) — for the seven days, leave your permanent residence and sit in a temporary one. Up to 20 amos a structure can be a temporary residence; above it, it can't.

script.speaker: Gemara
script.gloss: We learned a parallel halachah in a mishnah in Eiruvin: an alleyway (mavoy) higher than 20 amos — one must diminish it. R' Yehuda: he need not.

script.speaker: Gemara asks
script.quote: מַאי שְׁנָא גַּבֵּי סוּכָּה דְּתָנֵי פְּסוּלָה, וּמַאי שְׁנָא גַּבֵּי מָבוֹי דְּתָנֵי תַּקַּנְתָּא?
script.gloss: What's different about a sukkah, that the Mishnah teaches it's simply unfit — and what's different about a mavoy, that the Mishnah teaches how to fix it?

script.speaker: Answer
script.quote: סוּכָּה דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, תָּנֵי פְּסוּלָה. מָבוֹי דְּרַבָּנַן, תָּנֵי תַּקַּנְתָּא.
script.gloss: A sukkah is a Torah-law (d'Oraisa) obligation, so the Mishnah teaches it's unfit. A mavoy is only rabbinic, so the Mishnah teaches the fix.

script.speaker: Alternative answer
script.quote: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: ... סוּכָּה דִּנְפִישִׁי מִילָּתַהּ — פָּסֵיק וְתָנֵי פְּסוּלָה, מָבוֹי דְּלָא נְפִישׁ מִילֵּיהּ — תָּנֵי תַּקַּנְתָּא.
script.gloss: Or: even for Torah law a fix could be taught — but a sukkah's requirements are numerous (size, walls, roofing), so the Mishnah just states "unfit" categorically rather than spelling out a remedy. A mavoy has few requirements, so the fix is stated directly.

script.speaker: Gemara asks
script.gloss: From where is this law — that a sukkah may not exceed 20 amos — derived?

script.speaker: Rabbah
script.quote: לְמַעַן יֵדְעוּ דוֹרוֹתֵיכֶם כִּי בַסּוּכּוֹת הוֹשַׁבְתִּי אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
script.gloss: Up to 20 amos, a person is aware he's residing in a sukkah — his eye catches the roofing without effort. Above 20 amos, a person isn't aware, because the eye doesn't catch sight of it.

script.speaker: Rebbi Zeira
script.gloss: Up to 20 amos, a person sits in the shade of the sukkah's roofing. Above 20 amos, a person sits in the shade of the walls instead — not the sukkah itself.

script.speaker: Abaye challenges
script.quote: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, הָעוֹשֶׂה סוּכָּתוֹ בְּעַשְׁתְּרוֹת קַרְנַיִם, הָכִי נָמֵי דְּלָא הָוֵי סוּכָּה?
script.gloss: If that's so, then one who builds his sukkah in Ashterot Karnayim — a spot shaded by mountains on both sides — should also not have a valid sukkah, since he's not sitting in the shade of his own roofing.

script.speaker: Rebbi Zeira answers
script.quote: הָתָם, דַּל עַשְׁתְּרוֹת קַרְנַיִם — אִיכָּא צֵל סוּכָּה. הָכָא, דַּל דְּפָנוֹת — לֵיכָּא צֵל סוּכָּה.
script.gloss: There, if you hypothetically remove the mountains, the sukkah's own roofing still gives shade. Here (an over-height sukkah), if you remove the walls, there's no shade from the roofing at all — the walls were doing all the work.

script.speaker: Rava
script.gloss: The Torah says: for all seven days, leave your permanent residence and sit in a temporary one. Up to 20 amos, a person can make his residence a temporary one; above that height, he can't — it becomes a permanent residence instead.

script.speaker: Abaye challenges
script.quote: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, עָשָׂה מְחִיצוֹת שֶׁל בַּרְזֶל וְסִיכֵּךְ עַל גַּבָּן, הָכִי נָמֵי דְּלָא הָוֵי סוּכָּה?
script.gloss: If that's so, then one who builds walls of iron and roofs over them should also not have a valid sukkah — but no one holds that.

script.speaker: Rava answers
script.quote: עַד עֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה דְּאָדָם עוֹשֶׂה דִּירָתוֹ דִּירַת עֲרַאי, כִּי עָבֵיד לֵיהּ דִּירַת קֶבַע — נָמֵי נָפֵיק. לְמַעְלָה מֵעֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה ... כִּי עָבֵיד לֵיהּ דִּירַת עֲרַאי — נָמֵי לָא נָפֵיק.
script.gloss: Up to 20 amos — the height where a person normally builds a temporary residence — even building it sturdily like a permanent one still fulfills the mitzvah. Above 20 amos — where a person normally builds a permanent residence — even building it flimsily like a temporary one does not.

tosfos.summary: Why the Gemara doesn't ask the same question about hadassim (myrtle branches).

points.label: (a) Implied Question
points.he: והא דלא פריך מאי שנא גבי הדס דתני פסולה ותקנתא...
points.en: The Gemara does not ask why hadassim are different, seeing as the Mishnah there (32b) says a hadas is invalid and then teaches how to fix it — "Or if its berries were more than its leaves, it is invalid; if he lessened the berries, it is valid" — unlike our Mishnah, which just says the sukkah is invalid with no fix given.

points.label: (b) Answer #1
points.he: דלא פריך אלא מסוכה ומבוי שדינם שוה לענין גבוה...
points.en: Our Gemara only asks the question about sukkah and mavoy, because their laws are similar regarding height, and even so each uses different terminology.

points.label: (c) Answer #2
points.he: ועוד דגבי הדס אצטריך למיתני תקנתא...
points.en: Additionally, by hadassim the Mishnah needed to state the fix — otherwise one might think that since it grew invalid to begin with, there's no way to fix it.

tosfos.summary: Why the Mishnah says sukkah is "invalid" rather than "lessen it," and how that squares with a similar teaching about Chanukah candles.

points.label: (a) Explanation #1
points.he: דאי הוה תני ימעט חיישינן דילמא טעי איניש...
points.en: If the Mishnah said "he should lessen it," one might mistakenly think it's fine lechatchilah not to, and b'dieved it's still valid. The Tana was careful with his wording lest a person come to transgress a Torah prohibition, so he wrote "invalid" — even though that's a less pleasant term than "he should lessen it." For mavoy, which is only rabbinic, he wasn't concerned, so he used the nicer term.

points.label: i. Proof
points.en: This is as we find in Pesachim (3a), that the Torah twists its own language rather than say something indelicate.

points.label: (b) Observation
points.en: Rashi does not give this explanation.

points.label: (c) Explanation #2
points.he: אי נמי יש לומר דלשון ימעט משמע חומרא דרבנן...
points.en: Alternatively, "he should lessen it" implies a mere rabbinic stringency, while "invalid" implies a Torah-level law.

points.label: (d) Implied Question
points.he: ובפרק במה מדליקין (שבת דף כב.) דאמרינן נר חנוכה...
points.en: In Shabbos (22a), Rebbi Tanchum says a Chanukah candle placed more than 20 amos high is invalid, like a sukkah and an alleyway — so why does that teaching use "invalid" instead of "he should lessen it," per the explanations above?

points.label: (e) Answer #1
points.he: אגב דתנן כסוכה נקט נמי גבי נר חנוכה פסולה
points.en: Since that teaching parallels the Mishnah in Sukkah, Rebbi Tanchum uses "invalid" there too.

points.label: (f) Answer #2
points.he: א״נ אי הוה תני ימעט הוה משמע כמות שהיתה מדלקת ישפילנה...
points.en: Alternatively, "lessen it" would imply lowering the candle while lit — which fails according to the opinion that the mitzvah is fulfilled only by the act of lighting in the proper place. And even per the opinion that placement fulfills the mitzvah, an onlooker might think he's lighting it there for mundane use.

tosfos.summary: Rabah's view on a sukkah with some sechach hanging down within 20 amos.

points.label: (a) Question
points.he: קצת קשה ללישנא קמא דבריש עירובין (דף ג.)...
points.en: This is somewhat difficult against the first version of the Gemara in Eruvin (3a): where some sechach hangs within 20 amos, Rabah says the sukkah is invalid — but the eye can still catch that lower sechach! (Our text does read "Rabah" there, not Rava, since Rava there argues and validates it.)

points.label: (b) Answer
points.he: ויש לומר דהא מפרש התם טעמא משום דסוכה דביחיד קא הוי...
points.en: A sukkah is usually built for one individual or family, who won't always remember to check for stray low sechach — sometimes that bit gets removed, leaving the whole sechach above 20 amos (though if it weren't removed, it would be valid min ha'Torah per Rabah). This also fits Ravina's answer there, that the Rabanan were stringent about sukkah specifically because it's a Torah law — implying that min ha'Torah it would be valid.

tosfos.summary: How Rava defines a sukkah that "can be temporary," and why rain on Sukkot is a bad omen even if boards could keep it out.

points.label: (a) Explanation
points.he: דאע״ג דיש לפרש קרא בדירה שאינה ראויה אלא לשבעה...
points.en: Even though the verse could be read as excluding only a permanent home, it's really teaching a measure — how tall a sukkah can be, i.e. a height at which it could still be built as a temporary structure.

points.label: (b) Question
points.he: וא״ת וכיון דלא חיישינן אלא שתהא ראויה לעשותה עראי...
points.en: Since we only require that the sukkah be capable of being temporary — even if this one is actually built permanently — why does the Gemara in Ta'anis (2a) call rain on Sukkot a bad omen? One could just nail boards over it to keep the rain out!

points.label: 1. Answer
points.he: ואפילו תימצי לומר דאסור משום גזרת תקרה...
points.en: One might say that's forbidden by the rabbinic decree against roofing with solid boards (as on 14a, regarding R' Meir and R' Yehuda's machloket about board-sechach: if valid, people would say "what's the difference between this and my own roof" — and one's house is certainly an invalid sukkah min ha'Torah).

points.label: 2. Question
points.he: מ״מ כיון דלא אסור אלא מדרבנן לא שייכא למימר שהגשמים סימן קללה
points.en: Even so, that's only a rabbinic-level prohibition — how can rain be called a bad "omen" over something only rabbinically forbidden?

points.label: (c) Answer
points.he: וי״ל דנהי דלא חיישינן בדפנות אי עביד להו קבע...
points.en: Even though we don't care if the walls are permanent, since a sukkah is defined mainly by its sechach, it's invalid unless the sechach itself is built in a removable, temporary way.

points.label: 1. Answer (cont.)
points.he: ומה״ט נמי ניחא לרבי זירא דדריש מדכתי׳ וסוכה תהיה לצל...
points.en: This also explains Rebbi Zeira's opinion: he derives from "the sukkah shall be for shade" — but the verse also mentions shelter from flood and rain, so shouldn't sukkot need to be rainproof? Rather, since the sechach must stay removable, it can't be sealed rainproof, or it would become permanent.
